Sixth grade science · Unit 4

Weather & the Water Cycle

The water in your glass has been rain, ocean, cloud, and ice before. Weather is the atmosphere moving that water around, powered by the Sun. By the end of this page you can explain why it rains, why the wind blows, and why Ann Arbor isn't Miami.

Where we left off: sunlight (Unit 1) is absorbed and becomes thermal energy (Unit 2), and heated air and water move in loops called convection. Warm fluids rise and cool fluids sink. That is what powers weather, and forces (Unit 3) such as air pressure and gravity steer it.

Concept 1 · The atmosphere

An ocean of air

We live at the bottom of an ocean of air. Air has mass and it flows like water, so the more air above you, the more pressure. Climb up and there is less air above you, so the air is thinner and the pressure is lower.

Analogy

Pressure under water, pressure under air

Dive to the bottom of a deep pool and your ears feel squeezed. All the water above you has weight, and because water is a fluid it presses on you from every side, not only from above. The deeper you go, the more water is above you, and the more pressure you feel. About 10 meters down, you feel twice the pressure you feel at the surface.

Air is a fluid too. It flows, it pours from high pressure to low pressure, and it presses on you from every side. We live at the bottom of an ocean of air that is tens of kilometers deep, and its weight is the air pressure you feel all the time. Walk up a mountain and there is less air above you, so there is less pressure.

Where it breaks: water has a clear top and is about equally dense all the way down. Air has no top. It gets thinner and thinner until it fades into space.

Try it

Rise through all five layers

Data

Pressure drops fast as you climb: fewer air particles

Air pressure comes from air particles (atoms and molecules) bumping into things. Higher up there are fewer particles in each cubic meter and less air above pushing down, so the pressure drops. Half of all the air is below about 5.5 km. Rounded teaching model.

Concept 2 · The water cycle

The same water, over and over

The Sun's energy drives the cycle: evaporation lifts water up, condensation makes clouds, precipitation brings it down, and collection sends it back. No water is made or lost, so the water in your glass is very old: some of it was probably once a dinosaur's drink.

Analogy

Your bathroom after a hot shower

Steam rises

Hot water turns to gas: evaporation.

Mirror fogs

Steam hits the cold mirror and turns to droplets: condensation.

Drips run down

Droplets get heavy and fall: precipitation.

In your bathroomIn nature
Hot shower waterOcean and lake water warmed by the Sun
Steam risingEvaporation: liquid water becomes invisible water vapor
Cold mirrorCold air high in the sky
Fog on the mirrorCondensation: vapor turns back into droplets, which form clouds
Drips running downPrecipitation: rain, snow, sleet or hail falling
Water pooling at the bottomCollection: rivers, lakes, oceans and groundwater

That mirror is a tiny water cycle. The Sun does the same job for the whole planet, and it has been running for billions of years.

Where is Earth's water?

ocean (salty) 97ice and glaciers 2groundwater 1

Out of every 100 drops of Earth's water, about 97 are in the oceans. Fresh lakes and rivers are less than one hundredth of one drop. We rely on a very small slice. (Rounded; groundwater is partly salty.)

Concept 3 · Pressure and fronts

Why the weather changes

Warm air is light and rises, which leaves low pressure behind. Cold air is heavy and sinks, which makes high pressure. Wind blows from high toward low, and a front is where a warm air mass and a cold air mass meet. A falling barometer usually means a storm is coming.

Diagram

Why warm air rises and cold air sinks

Air is made of tiny particles that are always moving. When air is warm, its particles move faster and push apart, so the air expands and the same amount of space holds fewer particles. It has less mass, so it is lighter and it rises. When air is cold, its particles move slowly and pack closer together, so the same size chunk has more mass. It is heavier and it sinks.

Where warm air rises, the air pushes down on the ground less, so the ground sees low pressure. Where cold air sinks, it pushes down more, so the ground sees high pressure. Air then moves from high pressure toward low pressure, and that moving air is wind. It is a bit like people drifting from a crowded room into an empty one.

Diagram

Cold front vs. warm front

A front is the edge of a moving air mass. The slope of that edge decides what kind of weather you get, so pick each type and compare the slope. (These pictures exaggerate the slopes. Real fronts are far flatter, but a cold front is steeper than a warm front.)

Data

Three days, one storm

Before you read the charts: a barometer measures air pressure. Pressure falls when warm, light air rises, and rises again when cold, heavy air moves in. These three charts are all measured in one place (like Ann Arbor) as a cold front from the previous diagram passes over it. Read them from top to bottom: first the pressure drops, then the temperature jumps up just before the front, then the front arrives with rain and the temperature plunges. Slide the hour to follow one storm from start to finish.

Made-up but realistic data for a cold front passing through. Warm before the front (southwest wind), then a sharp drop in temperature, rising pressure, and clearing after.

Concept 4 · Why the wind blows

Sun heats ground unevenly

Land warms and cools faster than water. The warm air over land rises, cool air from the water rushes in, and that is a sea breeze. At night the pattern flips.

Analogy

A parked car on a sunny day

Leave a metal seat-belt buckle and a bottle of water in a parked car. After an hour the buckle is too hot to touch, but the water is only warm. Same sunshine, same time. Water needs about four to five times as much energy as rock, soil or metal to warm up by the same amount, and water also mixes and lets sunlight in deeper, so it heats up and cools down slowly. Land is like the buckle and the lake or ocean is like the bottle.

Now add air: air over the hot land warms and rises, and cooler air from over the water slides in to replace it. That sliding air is the sea breeze. At night the land cools quickly while the water stays warmer, the pattern flips, and the breeze blows the other way.

Where it breaks: a beach is not a car seat. The Sun heats the sand only on top, and the ocean is deep, so the real ocean stores far more heat than a bottle.

Try it

Beach through the day

Data

Land swings, water barely moves

This chart follows one summer day. The tan line is land and the blue line is water. Look at how tall each swing is.

The shaded orange stretch is when land is warmer, so a sea breeze blows in. The shaded blue stretch is when water is warmer, so a land breeze blows out. Where the lines cross, the breeze switches. Land swings about 16 °C in a day while the water changes only about 3 °C. Teaching values.

Build it

Engineering challenge: the cup anemometer

The problem: build a spinning anemometer that counts wind speed by how fast it turns in front of a fan.

Criteria: spins freely, and gives roughly the same count (within 2) on two tries at the same fan speed.

Constraints: 4 small cups, 2 straws, 1 pencil, a pin or paperclip for the axle, and tape.

  1. Try it in the game first. Play Droplet's Journey at the bottom of this page. Notice how the wind keeps pushing in one direction.
  2. Plan. Sketch two different ideas on your design log. Think about why the cups all face the same way and why the pivot needs to spin with as little friction as possible.
  3. Build and test. Count rotations for 20 seconds at low fan speed, then at high fan speed. Repeat each speed once to check your count.
  4. Improve. Change one thing, test again, and record it.

Print a design log for each team. Real anemometers use this exact idea: count spins in a fixed time, and faster wind means more spins.

Concept 5 · Weather vs climate

One day vs. thirty years

Weather is what the atmosphere is doing today. Climate is the pattern over many years, usually 30 or more. Climate tells you what to pack; weather tells you what to wear today.

Analogy

Mood vs. personality

One grumpy Tuesday doesn't make someone a grumpy person. One cold day doesn't change the climate. Climate is the average of thousands of days, just as personality is the pattern across thousands of moods.

Weather is what you see out the window on one day: today's temperature, rain and wind. Climate is that pattern averaged over many years, at least 30 by the usual definition. Scientists use such a long stretch so that a few unusual days or years do not hide the pattern. Climate tells you what usually happens in a place, for example that Ann Arbor has snowy winters and warm summers. Weather tells you what is happening right now.

Data

Average monthly temperature (°F)

Approximate 30-year monthly averages. One hot April day is weather. It does not move the line, which is climate.

Diagram

The greenhouse effect

Amount of greenhouse gasHeat sent back downAverage temperature
Nonenone: all the heat escapesabout -18 °C (0 °F), frozen
Today's levelpart of it comes backabout 15 °C (59 °F)
Much moreeven more comes backwarmer than 15 °C

Sunlight passes through the air and is absorbed by the ground. The warm ground gives off invisible heat rays. Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and water vapor absorb some of those rays, then give the energy off again in every direction, so part of it heads back down. Nothing is sealed in like a lid: heat still escapes to space, just more slowly. Without any, Earth's average would be about -18 °C (0 °F) instead of about 15 °C (59 °F).

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

Explain why a breeze blows off the lake on a hot afternoon, and how the lake is part of the water cycle.

Show a model answer

Land heats faster than water, so air above land warms, expands, and rises, leaving low pressure. Cooler air from the lake flows in to fill the gap, which is the breeze.

The Sun evaporates lake water into water vapor. High in the air it cools and condenses into clouds, and then falls as rain or snow that runs back into the lake: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection.

Words to know

atmosphere
The layer of gases around Earth.
air pressure
The push of air's weight on everything below it.
evaporation
Liquid water turning into water vapor.
condensation
Water vapor turning into liquid droplets.
precipitation
Water falling as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
dew point
The temperature at which air gets so cool that water vapor condenses.
front
Boundary between two air masses.
sea breeze
Daytime wind from cool water to warm land.
weather
Atmosphere conditions at a place and time.
climate
Typical weather pattern over 30 or more years.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $10): a clear jar, ice, hot water, hairspray or a match for the cloud-in-a-jar demo, a metal can, a balloon, a bottle, thermometers, sand and water in two trays, a lamp. For the cup anemometer: 4 small cups, 2 straws, a pencil, a pin or paperclip, and a fan.

  • Concept 1: blow up a balloon, tie it, put it in a bag, and squeeze: air takes up space and presses back. A quick balloon-on-bottle barometer works.
  • Concept 2: make a cloud in a jar with hot water, a plate of ice on top, and a squirt of aerosol. Sweat a cold can.
  • Concept 3: record pressure from a weather app each hour for a day.
  • Concept 4: put sand and water under a lamp and compare temperatures every minute for 10 minutes. Then run the cup anemometer challenge (about 30 to 40 minutes).
  • Concept 5: print a month of daily highs for your town and draw the average line.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Clouds are made of smoke or cotton." They are billions of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.
  • "Rain comes from clouds holding all the water at once." It falls when droplets collide and get heavy.
  • "Cold weather today disproves climate change." It confuses weather with climate.
  • "The greenhouse effect is bad." It's natural and necessary. The concern is adding too much.
  • "Greenhouse gases put a lid on the heat." They absorb heat rays and send some back down; heat still leaves for space, just more slowly.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions.
